Reference: Goodman-Bacon (2021)

Model Setting

The paper studies the two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences estimator (TWFEDD) when units receive a binary treatment at different times. The canonical difference-in-differences (DD) design has two groups and two periods, and its estimate is a difference of four sample means, so it is clear which comparisons generate the estimate and what leads to bias. Most applications instead exploit variation in treatment timing and estimate a regression with unit fixed effects, time fixed effects and a treatment dummy. Before this paper it was not known precisely how that regression compares mean outcomes across groups, what treatment effect parameter it identifies, what the identifying assumption is, or why estimates change across specifications.

The main result is the DD decomposition theorem: the TWFEDD estimator equals a weighted average of all possible two-group/two-period (2x2) DD estimators in the data. Some 2x2 DDs compare a group treated at a given time with untreated units. Others compare two groups treated at different times, using the later-treated group as a control before its treatment begins, and the earlier-treated group as a control after its own treatment has begun. The weights are positive, sum to one, and are proportional to group sizes and to the variance of the treatment dummy in each pair, which is highest for units treated in the middle of the panel. Writing the 2x2 DDs in potential outcomes shows that the probability limit of the estimator is a variance-weighted average treatment effect on the treated (VWATT), plus a variance-weighted common trends term (VWCT), minus a term ΔATT\Delta\text{ATT}ΔATT that collects changes over time in the treatment effects of already-treated units that serve as controls. A causal interpretation therefore requires both a parallel trends assumption and treatment effects that are constant over time. The paper also provides diagnostic tools (a plot of the 2x2 DDs against their weights, weights for balance tests, a decomposition of the difference between two specifications, and an analysis of time-varying controls) and applies them to the effect of unilateral divorce laws on female suicide studied by Stevenson and Wolfers (2006). There the TWFEDD estimate is −3.08-3.08−3.08 suicides per million women, 37 percent of the weight falls on timing comparisons, and the comparisons that use already-treated states as controls are positive on average (3.51), so the estimate understates the average post-treatment effect of about −5-5−5.

Two-Way Fixed Effects Regression

With two groups and two periods the DD estimate is the coefficient on the interaction of a treatment group dummy and a post-period dummy:

yit=γ+γi⋅TREATi+γ⋅tPOSTt+β2x2TREATi×POSTt+uit(1)y_{it}=\gamma+\gamma_{i\cdot}TREAT_i+\gamma_{\cdot t}POST_t+\beta^{2x2}TREAT_i\times POST_t+u_{it} \tag{1}yit​=γ+γi⋅​TREATi​+γ⋅t​POSTt​+β2x2TREATi​×POSTt​+uit​(1)

When treatment timing varies, the post-period dummy is not defined for control observations, and researchers estimate a regression with dummies for cross-sectional units, dummies for time periods and a treatment dummy DitD_{it}Dit​:

yit=αi⋅+α⋅t+βDDDit+eit(2)y_{it}=\alpha_{i\cdot}+\alpha_{\cdot t}+\beta^{DD}D_{it}+e_{it} \tag{2}yit​=αi⋅​+α⋅t​+βDDDit​+eit​(2)

The data are a balanced panel with TTT periods ttt and NNN units iii. In the leading example each unit belongs to one of three timing groups: an early treatment group kkk that receives the treatment at ti=kt_i=kti​=k, a late treatment group ℓ\ellℓ treated at ti=ℓ>kt_i=\ell>kti​=ℓ>k, and an untreated group UUU with ti=∞t_i=\inftyti​=∞. Treatment is absorbing, so Dit=1D_{it}=1Dit​=1 for all t≥tit\geq t_it≥ti​. The sample share of timing group kkk is nk≡∑i1{ti=k}/Nn_k\equiv\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{t_i=k\}/Nnk​≡∑i​1{ti​=k}/N and the share of time it spends treated is Dˉk≡∑t1{t≥k}/T\bar{D}_k\equiv\sum_t\mathbf{1}\{t\geq k\}/TDˉk​≡∑t​1{t≥k}/T. The mean outcome of the units treated at date bbb during the post-period of treatment date aaa is:

yˉbPOST(a)≡1T−(a−1)∑t=aT[∑iyit1{ti=b}∑i1{ti=b}](3)\bar{y}^{\text{POST}(a)}_b\equiv\frac{1}{T-(a-1)}\sum_{t=a}^{T}\left[\frac{\sum_iy_{it}\mathbf{1}\{t_i=b\}}{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{t_i=b\}}\right] \tag{3}yˉ​bPOST(a)​≡T−(a−1)1​t=a∑T​[∑i​1{ti​=b}∑i​yit​1{ti​=b}​](3)

and yˉbPRE(a)\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}(a)}_byˉ​bPRE(a)​ is defined in the same way over the periods before aaa. Three windows matter in the example: PRE(k)\text{PRE}(k)PRE(k), the periods before kkk; MID(k,ℓ)\text{MID}(k,\ell)MID(k,ℓ), the periods from kkk to ℓ−1\ell-1ℓ−1 in which only group kkk is treated; and POST(ℓ)\text{POST}(\ell)POST(ℓ), the periods from ℓ\ellℓ to TTT. By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, β^DD\hat{\beta}^{DD}β^​DD equals the univariate regression coefficient of yity_{it}yit​ on the treatment dummy with unit and time means removed:

β^DD=C^(yit,D~it)V^D=1NT∑i∑tyitD~it1NT∑i∑tD~it2(4)\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\frac{\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{D}_{it}\right)}{\hat{V}^D}=\frac{\frac{1}{NT}\sum_i\sum_ty_{it}\tilde{D}_{it}}{\frac{1}{NT}\sum_i\sum_t\tilde{D}^2_{it}} \tag{4}β^​DD=V^DC^(yit​,D~it​)​=NT1​∑i​∑t​D~it2​NT1​∑i​∑t​yit​D~it​​(4)

where for any variable x~it=(xit−xˉi)−(xˉt−xˉˉ)\tilde{x}_{it}=\left(x_{it}-\bar{x}_i\right)-\left(\bar{x}_t-\bar{\bar{x}}\right)x~it​=(xit​−xˉi​)−(xˉt​−xˉˉ), with xˉi\bar{x}_ixˉi​ the unit mean, xˉt\bar{x}_txˉt​ the period mean and xˉˉ\bar{\bar{x}}xˉˉ the grand mean, and V^D\hat{V}^DV^D is the variance of D~it\tilde{D}_{it}D~it​.

The 2x2 Estimators in the Three-Group Case

With three groups one can form four simple designs in which the treatment status of one group changes and that of the other does not. Here 2x2 refers to two groups and two time windows, not two periods. If only one treated group and the untreated group are kept, the estimator is the canonical treated versus untreated comparison:

β^jU2x2≡(yˉjPOST(j)−yˉjPRE(j))−(yˉUPOST(j)−yˉUPRE(j)),j=k,ℓ(5)\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{jU}\equiv\left(\bar{y}^{\text{POST}(j)}_j-\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}(j)}_j\right)-\left(\bar{y}^{\text{POST}(j)}_U-\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}(j)}_U\right),\qquad j=k,\ell \tag{5}β^​jU2x2​≡(yˉ​jPOST(j)​−yˉ​jPRE(j)​)−(yˉ​UPOST(j)​−yˉ​UPRE(j)​),j=k,ℓ(5)

Without untreated units, identification comes only from differential timing. Before ℓ\ellℓ, the early group changes treatment status and the late group is a not-yet-treated control, which gives the earlier versus later comparison:

β^kℓ2x2,k≡(yˉkMID(k,ℓ)−yˉkPRE(k))−(yˉℓMID(k,ℓ)−yˉℓPRE(k))(6)\hat{\beta}^{2x2,k}_{k\ell}\equiv\left(\bar{y}^{\text{MID}(k,\ell)}_k-\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}(k)}_k\right)-\left(\bar{y}^{\text{MID}(k,\ell)}_\ell-\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}(k)}_\ell\right) \tag{6}β^​kℓ2x2,k​≡(yˉ​kMID(k,ℓ)​−yˉ​kPRE(k)​)−(yˉ​ℓMID(k,ℓ)​−yˉ​ℓPRE(k)​)(6)

After kkk, the late group changes treatment status and the early group does not, which gives the later versus earlier comparison:

β^kℓ2x2,ℓ≡(yˉℓPOST(ℓ)−yˉℓMID(k,ℓ))−(yˉkPOST(ℓ)−yˉkMID(k,ℓ))(7)\hat{\beta}^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}\equiv\left(\bar{y}^{\text{POST}(\ell)}_\ell-\bar{y}^{\text{MID}(k,\ell)}_\ell\right)-\left(\bar{y}^{\text{POST}(\ell)}_k-\bar{y}^{\text{MID}(k,\ell)}_k\right) \tag{7}β^​kℓ2x2,ℓ​≡(yˉ​ℓPOST(ℓ)​−yˉ​ℓMID(k,ℓ)​)−(yˉ​kPOST(ℓ)​−yˉ​kMID(k,ℓ)​)(7)

In the last comparison the already-treated units of group kkk serve as controls even though they are treated, because their treatment status does not change. Each 2x2 DD relates to the full sample in two ways. First, it uses a fraction of the NTNTNT observations: nk+nUn_k+n_Unk​+nU​ and nℓ+nUn_\ell+n_Unℓ​+nU​ for the two treated versus untreated terms, (nk+nℓ)(1−Dˉℓ)(n_k+n_\ell)(1-\bar{D}_\ell)(nk​+nℓ​)(1−Dˉℓ​) for the earlier versus later term (the pre-period of group ℓ\ellℓ), and (nk+nℓ)Dˉk(n_k+n_\ell)\bar{D}_k(nk​+nℓ​)Dˉk​ for the later versus earlier term (the post-period of group kkk). Second, the amount of identifying variation is the variance of the fixed-effects-adjusted treatment dummy in the subsample:

V^jUD≡njU(1−njU)Dˉj(1−Dˉj),j=k,ℓV^kℓD,k≡nkℓ(1−nkℓ)Dˉk−Dˉℓ1−Dˉℓ1−Dˉk1−DˉℓV^kℓD,ℓ≡nkℓ(1−nkℓ)DˉℓDˉkDˉk−DˉℓDˉk(8)\begin{aligned} \hat{V}^D_{jU}&\equiv n_{jU}\left(1-n_{jU}\right)\bar{D}_j\left(1-\bar{D}_j\right),\qquad j=k,\ell\\ \hat{V}^{D,k}_{k\ell}&\equiv n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)\frac{\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell}{1-\bar{D}_\ell}\frac{1-\bar{D}_k}{1-\bar{D}_\ell}\\ \hat{V}^{D,\ell}_{k\ell}&\equiv n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)\frac{\bar{D}_\ell}{\bar{D}_k}\frac{\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell}{\bar{D}_k} \end{aligned} \tag{8}V^jUD​V^kℓD,k​V^kℓD,ℓ​​≡njU​(1−njU​)Dˉj​(1−Dˉj​),j=k,ℓ≡nkℓ​(1−nkℓ​)1−Dˉℓ​Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​​1−Dˉℓ​1−Dˉk​​≡nkℓ​(1−nkℓ​)Dˉk​Dˉℓ​​Dˉk​Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​​​(8)

where nab≡na/(na+nb)n_{ab}\equiv n_a/(n_a+n_b)nab​≡na​/(na​+nb​) is the relative size of the two groups in a pair. The first factor measures how balanced the two groups are and vanishes when there is no treatment group or no control group. The second factor is the variance over time of the treatment dummy of the pair's treatment group within its window, which is why the shares of time are rescaled in the two timing terms; it vanishes when treatment does not vary over time.

The Decomposition Theorem

Theorem 1 assumes that the data contain k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,Kk=1,…,K timing groups ordered by the time at which they receive a binary treatment, and possibly one group UUU that never receives it. Then the OLS estimate of the two-way fixed effects regression is a weighted average of all possible 2x2 DD estimators:

β^DD=∑k≠UskUβ^kU2x2+∑k≠U∑ℓ>k[skℓkβ^kℓ2x2,k+skℓℓβ^kℓ2x2,ℓ](9)\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\sum_{k\neq U}s_{kU}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{kU}+\sum_{k\neq U}\sum_{\ell>k}\left[s^k_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2,k}_{k\ell}+s^\ell_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}\right] \tag{9}β^​DD=k=U∑​skU​β^​kU2x2​+k=U∑​ℓ>k∑​[skℓk​β^​kℓ2x2,k​+skℓℓ​β^​kℓ2x2,ℓ​](9)

where the 2x2 DDs are the three expressions in sample means given above, applied to every group and every pair of groups, and the weights are:

skU=(nk+nU)2nkU(1−nkU)Dˉk(1−Dˉk)V^Dskℓk=((nk+nℓ)(1−Dˉℓ))2nkℓ(1−nkℓ)Dˉk−Dˉℓ1−Dˉℓ1−Dˉk1−DˉℓV^Dskℓℓ=((nk+nℓ)Dˉk)2nkℓ(1−nkℓ)DˉℓDˉkDˉk−DˉℓDˉkV^D(10)\begin{aligned} s_{kU}&=\frac{\left(n_k+n_U\right)^2n_{kU}\left(1-n_{kU}\right)\bar{D}_k\left(1-\bar{D}_k\right)}{\hat{V}^D}\\ s^k_{k\ell}&=\frac{\left(\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)\left(1-\bar{D}_\ell\right)\right)^2n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)\frac{\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell}{1-\bar{D}_\ell}\frac{1-\bar{D}_k}{1-\bar{D}_\ell}}{\hat{V}^D}\\ s^\ell_{k\ell}&=\frac{\left(\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)\bar{D}_k\right)^2n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)\frac{\bar{D}_\ell}{\bar{D}_k}\frac{\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell}{\bar{D}_k}}{\hat{V}^D} \end{aligned} \tag{10}skU​skℓk​skℓℓ​​=V^D(nk​+nU​)2nkU​(1−nkU​)Dˉk​(1−Dˉk​)​=V^D((nk​+nℓ​)(1−Dˉℓ​))2nkℓ​(1−nkℓ​)1−Dˉℓ​Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​​1−Dˉℓ​1−Dˉk​​​=V^D((nk​+nℓ​)Dˉk​)2nkℓ​(1−nkℓ​)Dˉk​Dˉℓ​​Dˉk​Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​​​​(10)

The weights sum to one. Each weight is the squared share of the subsample in all observations times the subsample variance V^kUD\hat{V}^D_{kU}V^kUD​, V^kℓD,k\hat{V}^{D,k}_{k\ell}V^kℓD,k​ or V^kℓD,ℓ\hat{V}^{D,\ell}_{k\ell}V^kℓD,ℓ​, divided by the overall variance. The weight is larger when the two groups are similar in size and when treatment occurs close to the middle of the relevant time window, that is, when Dˉk\bar{D}_kDˉk​, (Dˉk−Dˉℓ)/(1−Dˉℓ)(\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell)/(1-\bar{D}_\ell)(Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​)/(1−Dˉℓ​) or Dˉℓ/Dˉk\bar{D}_\ell/\bar{D}_kDˉℓ​/Dˉk​ is close to 0.5. With KKK timing groups there are K2−KK^2-KK2−K timing-only terms, and with an untreated group KKK further terms, so the estimator is built from K2K^2K2 distinct 2x2 DDs. Units treated before the first period (always-treated units) enter exactly like untreated units: their fixed-effects-adjusted treatment does not vary, so they only ever act as controls in terms like β^kU2x2\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{kU}β^​kU2x2​.

The proof (Appendix A) starts from the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell expression. Because DitD_{it}Dit​ varies only by timing group and period, the covariance of yity_{it}yit​ with D~it\tilde{D}_{it}D~it​ collapses to group-by-period means. A lemma rewrites the covariance with a two-way demeaned variable as a sum over every pair of groups, weighted by the product of their shares, of the period-by-period products of the between-group difference in outcomes and the between-group difference in demeaned treatment. For a pair with an untreated group this sum equals β^kU2x2Dˉk(1−Dˉk)\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{kU}\bar{D}_k(1-\bar{D}_k)β^​kU2x2​Dˉk​(1−Dˉk​). For two treated groups the difference in demeaned treatment takes three values across the three windows, and regrouping yields a term in β^kℓ2x2,k\hat{\beta}^{2x2,k}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2,k​ and a term in β^kℓ2x2,ℓ\hat{\beta}^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2,ℓ​. Replacing yity_{it}yit​ by DitD_{it}Dit​ makes every 2x2 DD equal to one, which shows that the numerators of the weights add up to V^D\hat{V}^DV^D.

The theorem also shows how the regression compares two treated groups. A two-group timing-only estimator is itself a weighted average of the two timing terms:

β^kℓ2x2≡μkℓβ^kℓ2x2,k+(1−μkℓ)β^kℓ2x2,ℓ,μkℓ=(1−Dˉℓ)2V^kℓD,k(1−Dˉℓ)2V^kℓD,k+Dˉk2V^kℓD,ℓ=1−Dˉk1−(Dˉk−Dˉℓ)(11)\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}\equiv\mu_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2,k}_{k\ell}+\left(1-\mu_{k\ell}\right)\hat{\beta}^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell},\qquad\mu_{k\ell}=\frac{\left(1-\bar{D}_\ell\right)^2\hat{V}^{D,k}_{k\ell}}{\left(1-\bar{D}_\ell\right)^2\hat{V}^{D,k}_{k\ell}+\bar{D}^2_k\hat{V}^{D,\ell}_{k\ell}}=\frac{1-\bar{D}_k}{1-\left(\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell\right)} \tag{11}β^​kℓ2x2​≡μkℓ​β^​kℓ2x2,k​+(1−μkℓ​)β^​kℓ2x2,ℓ​,μkℓ​=(1−Dˉℓ​)2V^kℓD,k​+Dˉk2​V^kℓD,ℓ​(1−Dˉℓ​)2V^kℓD,k​​=1−(Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​)1−Dˉk​​(11)

The weight μkℓ\mu_{k\ell}μkℓ​ falls as Dˉk\bar{D}_kDˉk​ approaches one, so the group treated closest to the middle of the panel gets more weight.

Numerical example and panel length. In the three-group example the groups are equally large, Dˉk=0.66\bar{D}_k=0.66Dˉk​=0.66 and Dˉℓ=0.16\bar{D}_\ell=0.16Dˉℓ​=0.16, and the treatment effect is 10 in group kkk and 15 in group ℓ\ellℓ. Since Dˉk(1−Dˉk)=0.22>0.13=Dˉℓ(1−Dˉℓ)\bar{D}_k(1-\bar{D}_k)=0.22>0.13=\bar{D}_\ell(1-\bar{D}_\ell)Dˉk​(1−Dˉk​)=0.22>0.13=Dˉℓ​(1−Dˉℓ​), the early group gets more weight in the comparisons with untreated units, and the earlier versus later term also gets more weight than the later versus earlier term (0.17 against 0.08 before scaling). The weights on β^kU2x2\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{kU}β^​kU2x2​, β^ℓU2x2\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{\ell U}β^​ℓU2x2​, β^kℓ2x2,k\hat{\beta}^{2x2,k}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2,k​ and β^kℓ2x2,ℓ\hat{\beta}^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2,ℓ​ are 0.37, 0.22, 0.28 and 0.13, and μkℓ=0.34/0.5=0.68\mu_{k\ell}=0.34/0.5=0.68μkℓ​=0.34/0.5=0.68. The estimate is 11.75 although the average effect is 12.5, because more weight falls on the early group, whose effect is smaller. Adding TTT periods to the end of the panel changes the shares of time treated to 0.83 and 0.58, so that group ℓ\ellℓ is now treated closer to the middle; the weights become 0.25, 0.43, 0.07 and 0.25, the terms in which group ℓ\ellℓ is the treatment group receive 68 percent instead of 35 percent of the weight, and the estimate becomes 13.4. Panel length alone can therefore change the estimate even when every 2x2 DD is unchanged.

Potential Outcomes and the 2x2 Estimands

Let Yit(k)Y_{it}(k)Yit​(k) be the outcome of unit iii in period ttt when it is treated at date kkk, and Yit(0)Y_{it}(0)Yit​(0) the untreated potential outcome, with Yit(ti)=Yit(0)Y_{it}(t_i)=Y_{it}(0)Yit​(ti​)=Yit​(0) for t<tit<t_it<ti​. The observed outcome is yit=DitYit(ti)+(1−Dit)Yit(0)y_{it}=D_{it}Y_{it}(t_i)+(1-D_{it})Y_{it}(0)yit​=Dit​Yit​(ti​)+(1−Dit​)Yit​(0). Because the regression averages outcomes over windows, the relevant parameter is the average treatment effect on the treated of timing group kkk over a window WWW with TWT_WTW​ periods:

ATTk(W)≡1TW∑t∈WE[Yit(k)−Yit(0)∣ti=k](12)\text{ATT}_k(W)\equiv\frac{1}{T_W}\sum_{t\in W}E\left[Y_{it}(k)-Y_{it}(0)\mid t_i=k\right] \tag{12}ATTk​(W)≡TW​1​t∈W∑​E[Yit​(k)−Yit​(0)∣ti​=k](12)

The change in average untreated potential outcomes of group kkk between two windows is:

ΔYk0(W1,W0)≡1TW1∑t∈W1E[Yit(0)∣ti=k]−1TW0∑t∈W0E[Yit(0)∣ti=k](13)\Delta Y^0_k\left(W_1,W_0\right)\equiv\frac{1}{T_{W_1}}\sum_{t\in W_1}E\left[Y_{it}(0)\mid t_i=k\right]-\frac{1}{T_{W_0}}\sum_{t\in W_0}E\left[Y_{it}(0)\mid t_i=k\right] \tag{13}ΔYk0​(W1​,W0​)≡TW1​​1​t∈W1​∑​E[Yit​(0)∣ti​=k]−TW0​​1​t∈W0​∑​E[Yit​(0)∣ti​=k](13)

Adding and subtracting average untreated outcomes of the treatment group shows that the probability limit of each 2x2 DD is an ATT plus a bias from differential trends:

βkU2x2=ATTk(POST(k))+[ΔYk0(POST(k),PRE(k))−ΔYU0(POST(k),PRE(k))]βkℓ2x2,k=ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))+[ΔYk0(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))−ΔYℓ0(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))]βkℓ2x2,ℓ=ATTℓ(POST(ℓ))+[ΔYℓ0(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))−ΔYk0(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))]−[ATTk(POST(ℓ))−ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))](14)\begin{aligned} \beta^{2x2}_{kU}&=\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{POST}(k)\right)+\left[\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{POST}(k),\text{PRE}(k)\right)-\Delta Y^0_U\left(\text{POST}(k),\text{PRE}(k)\right)\right]\\ \beta^{2x2,k}_{k\ell}&=\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)+\left[\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell),\text{PRE}(k)\right)-\Delta Y^0_\ell\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell),\text{PRE}(k)\right)\right]\\ \beta^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}&=\text{ATT}_\ell\left(\text{POST}(\ell)\right)+\left[\Delta Y^0_\ell\left(\text{POST}(\ell),\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)-\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{POST}(\ell),\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)\right]\\ &\quad-\left[\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{POST}(\ell)\right)-\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)\right] \end{aligned} \tag{14}βkU2x2​βkℓ2x2,k​βkℓ2x2,ℓ​​=ATTk​(POST(k))+[ΔYk0​(POST(k),PRE(k))−ΔYU0​(POST(k),PRE(k))]=ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ))+[ΔYk0​(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))−ΔYℓ0​(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))]=ATTℓ​(POST(ℓ))+[ΔYℓ0​(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))−ΔYk0​(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))]−[ATTk​(POST(ℓ))−ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ))]​(14)

In the first two lines common trends involve only untreated potential outcomes. In the third, the control group is already treated, so the change in its outcome contains the change in its own treatment effect between the two windows, and this change is subtracted.

The TWFEDD Estimand: VWATT, VWCT and Delta-ATT

Substituting these expressions into the decomposition theorem, with TTT fixed and NNN growing, gives:

plimN→∞ β^DD=βDD=VWATT+VWCT−ΔATT(15)\underset{N\rightarrow\infty}{\text{plim}}\,\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\beta^{DD}=\text{VWATT}+\text{VWCT}-\Delta\text{ATT} \tag{15}N→∞plim​β^​DD=βDD=VWATT+VWCT−ΔATT(15)

The first term is the variance-weighted average treatment effect on the treated:

VWATT≡∑k≠UσkUATTk(POST(k))+∑k≠U∑ℓ>k[σkℓkATTk(MID(k,ℓ))+σkℓℓATTℓ(POST(ℓ))](16)\text{VWATT}\equiv\sum_{k\neq U}\sigma_{kU}\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{POST}(k)\right)+\sum_{k\neq U}\sum_{\ell>k}\left[\sigma^k_{k\ell}\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)+\sigma^\ell_{k\ell}\text{ATT}_\ell\left(\text{POST}(\ell)\right)\right] \tag{16}VWATT≡k=U∑​σkU​ATTk​(POST(k))+k=U∑​ℓ>k∑​[σkℓk​ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ))+σkℓℓ​ATTℓ​(POST(ℓ))](16)

where σkU\sigma_{kU}σkU​, σkℓk\sigma^k_{k\ell}σkℓk​ and σkℓℓ\sigma^\ell_{k\ell}σkℓℓ​ are the probability limits of the decomposition weights. VWATT is a positively weighted average of the ATTs of the treatment groups over the post-windows of the 2x2 DDs. The second term is variance-weighted common trends:

VWCT≡∑k≠UσkU[ΔYk0(POST(k),PRE(k))−ΔYU0(POST(k),PRE(k))]+∑k≠U∑ℓ>k[σkℓk{ΔYk0(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))−ΔYℓ0(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))}+σkℓℓ{ΔYℓ0(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))−ΔYk0(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))}](17)\begin{aligned} \text{VWCT}\equiv&\sum_{k\neq U}\sigma_{kU}\left[\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{POST}(k),\text{PRE}(k)\right)-\Delta Y^0_U\left(\text{POST}(k),\text{PRE}(k)\right)\right]\\ &+\sum_{k\neq U}\sum_{\ell>k}\Big[\sigma^k_{k\ell}\left\{\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell),\text{PRE}(k)\right)-\Delta Y^0_\ell\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell),\text{PRE}(k)\right)\right\}\\ &+\sigma^\ell_{k\ell}\left\{\Delta Y^0_\ell\left(\text{POST}(\ell),\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)-\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{POST}(\ell),\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)\right\}\Big] \end{aligned} \tag{17}VWCT≡​k=U∑​σkU​[ΔYk0​(POST(k),PRE(k))−ΔYU0​(POST(k),PRE(k))]+k=U∑​ℓ>k∑​[σkℓk​{ΔYk0​(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))−ΔYℓ0​(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))}+σkℓℓ​{ΔYℓ0​(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))−ΔYk0​(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))}]​(17)

It generalizes common trends to a design with timing variation: the counterfactual trend of one timing group enters many 2x2 DDs, by different amounts and with opposite signs depending on whether the group is the treatment or the control group. The last term is a weighted sum of the changes in the treatment effects of each timing group before and after a later treatment date:

ΔATT≡∑k≠U∑ℓ>kσkℓℓ[ATTk(POST(ℓ))−ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))](18)\Delta\text{ATT}\equiv\sum_{k\neq U}\sum_{\ell>k}\sigma^\ell_{k\ell}\left[\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{POST}(\ell)\right)-\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)\right] \tag{18}ΔATT≡k=U∑​ℓ>k∑​σkℓℓ​[ATTk​(POST(ℓ))−ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ))](18)

This term is zero when average treatment effects are constant over time. When they are not, it is a bias relative to VWATT even if VWCT=0\text{VWCT}=0VWCT=0, and it is the source of the negative weights found by Borusyak and Jaravel (2017) and de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2020). The paper treats it as a bias and not as part of the estimand, because it arises from the way the regression forms its control group; the research design itself is not invalid, and event-study, stacked or reweighting estimators may be more appropriate. Always-treated units can also contribute: their 2x2 DDs use all periods and carry large weights, so changing effects in those units can dominate ΔATT\Delta\text{ATT}ΔATT.

Interpreting VWATT under Heterogeneity

Constant effects. If ATTk(W)=ATT\text{ATT}_k(W)=\text{ATT}ATTk​(W)=ATT for all groups and windows, then ΔATT=0\Delta\text{ATT}=0ΔATT=0 and VWATT=ATT\text{VWATT}=\text{ATT}VWATT=ATT. The remaining cases assume VWCT=0\text{VWCT}=0VWCT=0.

Effects that vary across units but not over time. If ATTk(W)=ATTk\text{ATT}_k(W)=\text{ATT}_kATTk​(W)=ATTk​, then ΔATT=0\Delta\text{ATT}=0ΔATT=0 still holds and:

VWATT=∑k≠UATTk[σkU+∑j=1k−1σjkk+∑j=k+1Kσkjk](19)\text{VWATT}=\sum_{k\neq U}\text{ATT}_k\left[\sigma_{kU}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\sigma^k_{jk}+\sum_{j=k+1}^{K}\sigma^k_{kj}\right] \tag{19}VWATT=k=U∑​ATTk​​σkU​+j=1∑k−1​σjkk​+j=k+1∑K​σkjk​​(19)

The term in brackets, denoted wkTw^T_kwkT​, is the sum of the weights of all 2x2 DDs in which group kkk is the treatment group. In general it differs from the group's sample share among treated units, nk/(1−nU)n_k/(1-n_U)nk​/(1−nU​), and it is not proportional to the share of time spent treated, so VWATT equals neither the sample ATT nor the effect in the average treated period. How far they differ depends on how effect heterogeneity is related to timing. Under Roy selection on gains, where treatment reaches the units with the largest effects first, the regression underestimates the sample-weighted ATT if treatment rolls out in the first half of the panel and overestimates it if treatment rolls out in the second half; reverse Roy selection gives the opposite conclusions. A simple check is to plot wkTw^T_kwkT​ against nk/(1−nU)n_k/(1-n_U)nk​/(1−nU​).

Effects that vary over time. Time-varying effects matter in two ways. They make the 2x2 DDs heterogeneous, because the terms average over different post-windows and short-run effects are up-weighted in the short windows between timing groups, so VWATT differs from the sample ATT. And they bias the estimate away from VWATT because ΔATT≠0\Delta\text{ATT}\neq0ΔATT=0. The paper illustrates this with identical counterfactual outcomes and a linear trend-break effect, Yit(ti)=Yit(0)+ϕ⋅(t−ti+1)Y_{it}(t_i)=Y_{it}(0)+\phi\cdot(t-t_i+1)Yit​(ti​)=Yit​(0)+ϕ⋅(t−ti​+1). The earlier versus later term identifies ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))=ϕ(ℓ−(k−1))/2\text{ATT}_k(\text{MID}(k,\ell))=\phi(\ell-(k-1))/2ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ))=ϕ(ℓ−(k−1))/2. The later versus earlier term is biased because the outcome of its control group kkk keeps growing:

β^kℓ2x2,ℓ=ϕT−ℓ+22−ϕT−(k−1)2=ϕk−ℓ+12≤0(20)\hat{\beta}^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}=\phi\frac{T-\ell+2}{2}-\phi\frac{T-(k-1)}{2}=\phi\frac{k-\ell+1}{2}\leq0 \tag{20}β^​kℓ2x2,ℓ​=ϕ2T−ℓ+2​−ϕ2T−(k−1)​=ϕ2k−ℓ+1​≤0(20)

where the first term is labelled ATTℓ(POST(ℓ))\text{ATT}_\ell(\text{POST}(\ell))ATTℓ​(POST(ℓ)) and the second is ΔATT/(1−μkℓ)\Delta\text{ATT}/(1-\mu_{k\ell})ΔATT/(1−μkℓ​), the change in the effect of group kkk between the two windows. This term is weakly negative although every treatment effect is positive and growing (the paper prints the first term as ϕT−(ℓ−1)2\phi\frac{T-(\ell-1)}{2}ϕ2T−(ℓ−1)​ and the result as ϕk−ℓ2\phi\frac{k-\ell}{2}ϕ2k−ℓ​, but its own footnote and the next equation use the exact average shown here). The bias carries over to the two-group timing estimate according to the relative weights:

β^kℓ2x2=ϕ[(2μkℓ−1)(ℓ−k)+1]2(21)\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}=\phi\frac{\left[\left(2\mu_{k\ell}-1\right)\left(\ell-k\right)+1\right]}{2} \tag{21}β^​kℓ2x2​=ϕ2[(2μkℓ​−1)(ℓ−k)+1]​(21)

Here μkℓ\mu_{k\ell}μkℓ​ and 1−μkℓ1-\mu_{k\ell}1−μkℓ​ are the weights on the two terms within the pair (the paper writes them as σkℓk\sigma^k_{k\ell}σkℓk​ and σkℓℓ\sigma^\ell_{k\ell}σkℓℓ​, which coincide with them only in a two-group sample). The whole estimate is wrong-signed when there is sufficiently more weight on the later versus earlier term, namely when (1−2μkℓ)(ℓ−k)>1(1-2\mu_{k\ell})(\ell-k)>1(1−2μkℓ​)(ℓ−k)>1. A single-coefficient specification therefore yields estimates of time-varying effects that are too small or even wrong-signed. The bias is specific to that specification: flexible event-study specifications may avoid it, and designs that match treated units to controls treated a fixed time later use only earlier versus later terms with a fixed post-period. The decomposition also explains why a linear trend common to all treated units cannot be estimated in timing-only designs: timing groups act as controls for each other, so permanent common trends difference out.

Identifying Assumption and Common Trends Weights

When ΔATT=0\Delta\text{ATT}=0ΔATT=0, identification of VWATT requires only VWCT=0\text{VWCT}=0VWCT=0, which is weaker than equal counterfactual trends in every pair. If average untreated potential outcomes of each group follow a linear trend, and ΔYk0\Delta Y^0_kΔYk0​ denotes the resulting difference in means between the windows of a 2x2 comparison (with a per-period slope the right side is multiplied by T/2T/2T/2), VWCT is approximately:

VWCT≈∑k≠UΔYk0[(σkU+∑j=1k−1σjkk+∑j=k+1Kσkjk)−(∑j=1k−1σjkj+∑j=k+1Kσkjj)]−ΔYU0∑k≠UσkU=∑kΔYk0[wkT−wkC](22)\begin{aligned} \text{VWCT}&\approx\sum_{k\neq U}\Delta Y^0_k\left[\left(\sigma_{kU}+\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\sigma^k_{jk}+\sum_{j=k+1}^{K}\sigma^k_{kj}\right)-\left(\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\sigma^j_{jk}+\sum_{j=k+1}^{K}\sigma^j_{kj}\right)\right]-\Delta Y^0_U\sum_{k\neq U}\sigma_{kU}\\ &=\sum_k\Delta Y^0_k\left[w^T_k-w^C_k\right] \end{aligned} \tag{22}VWCT​≈k=U∑​ΔYk0​​​σkU​+j=1∑k−1​σjkk​+j=k+1∑K​σkjk​​−​j=1∑k−1​σjkj​+j=k+1∑K​σkjj​​​−ΔYU0​k=U∑​σkU​=k∑​ΔYk0​[wkT​−wkC​]​(22)

where wkC≡∑j=1k−1σjkj+∑j=k+1Kσkjjw^C_k\equiv\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\sigma^j_{jk}+\sum_{j=k+1}^{K}\sigma^j_{kj}wkC​≡∑j=1k−1​σjkj​+∑j=k+1K​σkjj​ is the total weight of the terms in which group kkk is the control group. A differential trend in group kkk biases the terms in which it is the treatment group in one direction and the terms in which it is the control group in the other, so its net contribution to the bias is proportional to wkT−wkCw^T_k-w^C_kwkT​−wkC​: positive when this difference is positive, negative when it is negative, and zero when it is zero. With equal group sizes the difference is an inverted U in the share of time treated. Groups treated in the middle of the panel have high treatment variance and act mostly as treatment groups; groups treated near either end get more weight as controls than as treatments, and in designs without untreated units they always do. This defines the effective control group of a timing-only design. The same weights give a balance test: because the regression weights groups by wkT−wkCw^T_k-w^C_kwkT​−wkC​ and not by sample shares, a test of whether a confounder or a pre-trend is balanced should weight the group means in the same way, which also allows a test to be built by hand when covariates are not observed at the frequency of the outcome.

Comparing Specifications

Write the theorem as the product of a vector of weights and a vector of 2x2 DDs, β^DD=s′β^2x2\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\mathbf{s}'\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}β^​DD=s′β^​2x2. If an alternative estimator can be written in the same form, β^altDD=salt′β^alt2x2\hat{\beta}^{DD}_{alt}=\mathbf{s}'_{alt}\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}_{alt}β^​altDD​=salt′​β^​alt2x2​, the difference between the two has the form of a Oaxaca-Blinder-Kitagawa decomposition:

β^altDD−β^DD=s′(β^alt2x2−β^2x2)+(salt′−s′)β^2x2+(salt′−s′)(β^alt2x2−β^2x2)(23)\hat{\beta}^{DD}_{alt}-\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\mathbf{s}'\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}_{alt}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}\right)+\left(\mathbf{s}'_{alt}-\mathbf{s}'\right)\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}+\left(\mathbf{s}'_{alt}-\mathbf{s}'\right)\left(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}_{alt}-\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{2x2}\right) \tag{23}β^​altDD​−β^​DD=s′(β^​alt2x2​−β^​2x2)+(salt′​−s′)β^​2x2+(salt′​−s′)(β^​alt2x2​−β^​2x2)(23)

The three terms are due to changes in the 2x2 DDs (consistent with confounding or with heterogeneity within groups), to changes in the weights (a change of estimand) and to their interaction. Dividing by the difference gives shares, and scatter plots of the 2x2 DDs and of the weights of one specification against those of the other show which terms drive each part. Dropping untreated units is equivalent to setting all skUs_{kU}skU​ to zero and rescaling the timing weights to sum to one. Population weighting changes the means inside each 2x2 DD and bases the decomposition weights on population shares instead of sample shares. Reweighting untreated units by a propensity score leaves the timing terms and the weights unchanged and only alters the treated versus untreated DDs. Region-by-year fixed effects preserve the form of the theorem but apply it within regions, so 2x2 DDs drop out when no region contains a given pair of timing groups. Unit-specific linear trends over-control when treatment effects vary over time; the paper proposes instead to fit linear trends by group in the pre-period only, subtract them from the outcome in all periods and estimate the uncontrolled regression, which is unaffected by effect dynamics and does not change the weights (the analysis is in Appendix B).

DD with Time-Varying Controls

Most applications add time-varying controls Xit\mathbf{X}_{it}Xit​:

yit=αi⋅+α⋅t+ΦXit+βDD∣XDit+eit(24)y_{it}=\alpha_{i\cdot}+\alpha_{\cdot t}+\Phi\mathbf{X}_{it}+\beta^{DD|X}D_{it}+e_{it} \tag{24}yit​=αi⋅​+α⋅t​+ΦXit​+βDD∣XDit​+eit​(24)

After removing unit and time means, a Frisch-Waugh-Lovell regression partials the controls out of the treatment dummy:

D~it=ΓX~it+d~it(25)\tilde{D}_{it}=\Gamma\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{it}+\tilde{d}_{it} \tag{25}D~it​=ΓX~it​+d~it​(25)

The fitted value p~it≡Γ^X~it\tilde{p}_{it}\equiv\hat{\Gamma}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{it}p~​it​≡Γ^X~it​ is a linear prediction of treatment status based on the sample-wide relationship between controls and treatment, and the covariate-adjusted treatment variable is d~it=D~it−p~it\tilde{d}_{it}=\tilde{D}_{it}-\tilde{p}_{it}d~it​=D~it​−p~​it​, so that:

β^DD∣X≡C^(yit,d~it)V^d=C^(yit,D~it−p~it)V^d(26)\hat{\beta}^{DD|X}\equiv\frac{\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{it}\right)}{\hat{V}^d}=\frac{\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{D}_{it}-\tilde{p}_{it}\right)}{\hat{V}^d} \tag{26}β^​DD∣X≡V^dC^(yit​,d~it​)​=V^dC^(yit​,D~it​−p~​it​)​(26)

While D~it\tilde{D}_{it}D~it​ varies only by timing group and period, p~it\tilde{p}_{it}p~​it​ generally varies across units in the same timing group and period. Adding and subtracting group-by-period means splits the adjusted treatment variable into a within component d~i(k)t\tilde{d}_{i(k)t}d~i(k)t​ and a between component d~kt\tilde{d}_{kt}d~kt​:

d~it=[(dit−dˉi)−(dˉkt−dˉk)]+[(dˉkt−dˉk)−(dˉt−dˉˉ)](27)\tilde{d}_{it}=\left[\left(d_{it}-\bar{d}_i\right)-\left(\bar{d}_{kt}-\bar{d}_k\right)\right]+\left[\left(\bar{d}_{kt}-\bar{d}_k\right)-\left(\bar{d}_t-\bar{\bar{d}}\right)\right] \tag{27}d~it​=[(dit​−dˉi​)−(dˉkt​−dˉk​)]+[(dˉkt​−dˉk​)−(dˉt​−dˉˉ)](27)

where the first bracket is d~i(k)t\tilde{d}_{i(k)t}d~i(k)t​ and the second is d~kt\tilde{d}_{kt}d~kt​. Substituting into the expression for the controlled coefficient gives:

β^DD∣X=C^(yit,d~i(k)t)+C^(yit,d~kt)V^d=V^wdV^dβ^wp+V^bdV^d[β^DDV^D−β^bpV^bpV^bd](28)\hat{\beta}^{DD|X}=\frac{\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{i(k)t}\right)+\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt}\right)}{\hat{V}^d}=\frac{\hat{V}^d_w}{\hat{V}^d}\hat{\beta}^p_w+\frac{\hat{V}^d_b}{\hat{V}^d}\left[\frac{\hat{\beta}^{DD}\hat{V}^D-\hat{\beta}^p_b\hat{V}^p_b}{\hat{V}^d_b}\right] \tag{28}β^​DD∣X=V^dC^(yit​,d~i(k)t​)+C^(yit​,d~kt​)​=V^dV^wd​​β^​wp​+V^dV^bd​​[V^bd​β^​DDV^D−β^​bp​V^bp​​](28)

Here V^wd\hat{V}^d_wV^wd​ is the variance of the within component, V^bd\hat{V}^d_bV^bd​ and V^bp\hat{V}^p_bV^bp​ are the variances of the between components d~kt\tilde{d}_{kt}d~kt​ and p~kt\tilde{p}_{kt}p~​kt​, Ω≡V^wd/V^d\Omega\equiv\hat{V}^d_w/\hat{V}^dΩ≡V^wd​/V^d is the share of identifying variation that comes from within-timing-group comparisons and 1−Ω=V^bd/V^d1-\Omega=\hat{V}^d_b/\hat{V}^d1−Ω=V^bd​/V^d. The within coefficient β^wp≡C^(yit,d~i(k)t)/V^wd\hat{\beta}^p_w\equiv\hat{C}(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{i(k)t})/\hat{V}^d_wβ^​wp​≡C^(yit​,d~i(k)t​)/V^wd​ compares units with the same treatment status but different predicted treatment paths; it is a source of identifying variation that does not exist without controls. The term in square brackets is the between coefficient β^bd≡C^(yit,d~kt)/V^bd\hat{\beta}^d_b\equiv\hat{C}(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt})/\hat{V}^d_bβ^​bd​≡C^(yit​,d~kt​)/V^bd​: it contains the unadjusted coefficient and subtracts β^bp\hat{\beta}^p_bβ^​bp​, the coefficient from a regression of the outcome on p~kt\tilde{p}_{kt}p~​kt​ and two-way fixed effects. The between coefficient decomposes into adjusted 2x2 terms by pairs of groups:

β^bd=∑k∑ℓ>k(nk+nℓ)2V^b,kℓdV^bd[V^kℓDβ^kℓ2x2−V^b,kℓpβ^b,kℓpV^b,kℓd](29)\hat{\beta}^d_b=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)^2\frac{\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}}{\hat{V}^d_b}\left[\frac{\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}-\hat{V}^p_{b,k\ell}\hat{\beta}^p_{b,k\ell}}{\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}}\right] \tag{29}β^​bd​=k∑​ℓ>k∑​(nk​+nℓ​)2V^bd​V^b,kℓd​​[V^b,kℓd​V^kℓD​β^​kℓ2x2​−V^b,kℓp​β^​b,kℓp​​](29)

where the factor before the brackets is the weight skℓb∣Xs^{b|X}_{k\ell}skℓb∣X​, the term in brackets is the adjusted 2x2 term β^b,kℓd\hat{\beta}^d_{b,k\ell}β^​b,kℓd​, and the variances and coefficients with subscript kℓk\ellkℓ come from each two-group subsample. The full decomposition is:

β^DD∣X=Ωβ^wp+(1−Ω)∑k∑ℓ>kskℓb∣Xβ^kℓ2x2∣d(30)\hat{\beta}^{DD|X}=\Omega\hat{\beta}^p_w+\left(1-\Omega\right)\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}s^{b|X}_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2|d}_{k\ell} \tag{30}β^​DD∣X=Ωβ^​wp​+(1−Ω)k∑​ℓ>k∑​skℓb∣X​β^​kℓ2x2∣d​(30)

in which the paper writes β^kℓ2x2∣d\hat{\beta}^{2x2|d}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2∣d​ for the adjusted 2x2 term. Controls thus change the estimate through both channels of the specification comparison: the weights are based on V^b,kℓd\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}V^b,kℓd​ instead of V^kℓD\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}V^kℓD​, and the 2x2 terms subtract the subsample relationship between the outcome and predicted treatment. The pairwise terms are not split into earlier versus later and later versus earlier parts, and they are not what one would obtain by estimating the controlled regression on each subsample, because they adjust by predicted treatment from the full sample. Covariates must be unaffected by the treatment. The paper concludes (with details in its appendix) that controls do not simply remove bias: they introduce within-group comparisons, extrapolate the full-sample prediction to pairwise components, partial out period-by-period covariance that could not have biased the uncontrolled estimate, and net out any part of the treatment effect correlated with covariate paths in the post-period.

Application: Unilateral Divorce and Female Suicide

The application replicates Stevenson and Wolfers (2006), who use the staggered adoption of unilateral (no-fault) divorce laws. The outcome is the age-adjusted female suicide rate per million women in a state-year panel from 1964 to 1996 without Alaska and Hawaii (mean 52). There are 12 timing groups with adoption years from 1969 to 1985, the largest being the 10 states of 1973 (nk=0.20n_k=0.20nk​=0.20, Dˉk=0.73\bar{D}_k=0.73Dˉk​=0.73); 5 non-reform states; and 8 states that reformed before 1964 and are treated throughout. The shares of time treated range from 0.85 for the 1969 states to 0.36 for the 1985 state. The baseline specification is unweighted and has no covariates.

  • Estimate: the event-study coefficients show no clear trend before adoption and fall afterwards. The TWFEDD coefficient is −3.08-3.08−3.08 (standard error 1.13 in the text and 1.27 in the table of specifications), a reduction of about 6 percent.

  • Decomposition plot: there are 156 distinct 2x2 DDs: 12 against pre-1964 reform states, 12 against non-reform states, 66 earlier versus later and 66 later versus earlier. The total weight and the weighted average 2x2 DD are 0.38 and −7.04-7.04−7.04 for comparisons with pre-1964 reform states, 0.24 and −5.33-5.33−5.33 for comparisons with non-reform states, 0.11 and −0.19-0.19−0.19 for earlier-treated versus later-treated controls, and 0.26 and 3.51 for later-treated versus earlier-treated controls. Timing terms carry 37 percent of the weight. Comparisons of the 1973 states with non-reform and pre-1964 reform states account for 18 percent, and the ten highest-weight terms for more than half.

  • Bias from time-varying effects: the average post-treatment event-study coefficient is −4.92-4.92−4.92, and the DD estimate is about 60 percent as large. The gap comes from the later versus earlier terms, which are positive on average because effects grow over time in the already-treated controls. Removing these terms from the weighted average gives −5.44-5.44−5.44. Dropping the untreated groups leaves only timing terms and gives (0.264/0.374)×3.51+(0.11/0.374)×(−0.19)=2.42(0.264/0.374)\times3.51+(0.11/0.374)\times(-0.19)=2.42(0.264/0.374)×3.51+(0.11/0.374)×(−0.19)=2.42, a sign reversal.

  • Common trends weights: the earliest groups get less weight than their sample shares. The 1970 states have wkT−wkC=0.0039w^T_k-w^C_k=0.0039wkT​−wkC​=0.0039 and the 1973 states 0.18; adding a trend of 5 per year to the outcome of the 1970 states moves the estimate only to −2.75-2.75−2.75, while adding it to the 1973 states gives 12.28. The 1969 states get more weight as controls than as treatments, and in the sample without untreated groups this holds for all states treated before 1973.

  • Alternative specifications: population weighting gives −0.35-0.35−0.35; of the difference of 2.73 from the baseline, 52 percent is due to the 2x2 DDs, 39 percent to the weights and 9 percent to the interaction, and the change is driven by terms involving the 1970 states (Iowa and California). Propensity score reweighting gives 1.04, entirely through the 2x2 DDs. Unit-specific trends give 0.59 (shares 0.90, 0.47 and −0.36-0.36−0.36), group-specific pre-trend adjustment gives −6.52-6.52−6.52 (entirely through the 2x2 DDs), and region-by-year fixed effects give −1.16-1.16−1.16 (shares 0.37, 0.76 and −0.13-0.13−0.13).

  • Controls: adding per-capita income, the female homicide rate and the welfare participation rate gives −2.52-2.52−2.52 (standard error 1.09). Of the difference of 0.56, 73 percent comes from the within term, 22 percent from the 2x2 DDs and 5 percent from the weights. The within coefficient is 80.01 and the within variation is small (the paper reports 0.005), so the within term adds 0.40. The controls predict treatment poorly, with an R-squared of 0.0067 in the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell regression, so the between terms barely move: the term for the 1970 states against non-reform states is −22.4-22.4−22.4 with controls and −22.3-22.3−22.3 without.

The paper concludes that the regression should be used with caution when timing varies: it has a causal interpretation only when VWCT=0\text{VWCT}=0VWCT=0 and ΔATT=0\Delta\text{ATT}=0ΔATT=0, and even then it delivers a variance-weighted parameter that may not be the one of interest.

References

  • Goodman-Bacon, Andrew. 2021. “Difference-in-Differences with Variation in Treatment Timing.” Journal of Econometrics, 225(2): 254–277.

This is the canonical two-group/two-period DD regression. TREATiTREAT_iTREATi​ equals one for units in the treatment group, POSTtPOST_tPOSTt​ equals one in the period after treatment, and their product is the treatment indicator. The four coefficients fit the four cell means exactly, because the regression is saturated:

E[yit∣TREATi=0,POSTt=0]=γ,E[yit∣TREATi=0,POSTt=1]=γ+γ⋅t,E[yit∣TREATi=1,POSTt=0]=γ+γi⋅,E[yit∣TREATi=1,POSTt=1]=γ+γi⋅+γ⋅t+β2x2.\begin{aligned} E\left[y_{it}\mid TREAT_i=0,POST_t=0\right]&=\gamma, &\qquad E\left[y_{it}\mid TREAT_i=0,POST_t=1\right]&=\gamma+\gamma_{\cdot t},\\ E\left[y_{it}\mid TREAT_i=1,POST_t=0\right]&=\gamma+\gamma_{i\cdot}, &\qquad E\left[y_{it}\mid TREAT_i=1,POST_t=1\right]&=\gamma+\gamma_{i\cdot}+\gamma_{\cdot t}+\beta^{2x2}. \end{aligned}E[yit​∣TREATi​=0,POSTt​=0]E[yit​∣TREATi​=1,POSTt​=0]​=γ,=γ+γi⋅​,​E[yit​∣TREATi​=0,POSTt​=1]E[yit​∣TREATi​=1,POSTt​=1]​=γ+γ⋅t​,=γ+γi⋅​+γ⋅t​+β2x2.​

Solving these four equations for the interaction coefficient shows that OLS returns a difference of four sample means:

β^2x2=(yˉTREATPOST−yˉTREATPRE)−(yˉCONTROLPOST−yˉCONTROLPRE).\hat{\beta}^{2x2}=\left(\bar{y}^{\text{POST}}_{\text{TREAT}}-\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}}_{\text{TREAT}}\right)-\left(\bar{y}^{\text{POST}}_{\text{CONTROL}}-\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}}_{\text{CONTROL}}\right).β^​2x2=(yˉ​TREATPOST​−yˉ​TREATPRE​)−(yˉ​CONTROLPOST​−yˉ​CONTROLPRE​).

The coefficient γi⋅\gamma_{i\cdot}γi⋅​ absorbs any permanent level difference between the groups and γ⋅t\gamma_{\cdot t}γ⋅t​ absorbs any change common to both, so the estimate is the change in the treatment group net of the change in the control group. It is transparent which comparison is made and what would bias it, namely a differential change in the two groups that is not caused by treatment. This transparency is the benchmark of the note: the 2x2 estimators in equations (5), (6) and (7) are exactly of this form, and the decomposition theorem in equation (9) expresses the regression with staggered timing as a weighted average of them.

This is the two-way fixed effects regression that researchers run when treatment starts at different dates. αi⋅\alpha_{i\cdot}αi⋅​ is a full set of unit dummies, α⋅t\alpha_{\cdot t}α⋅t​ a full set of period dummies, and DitD_{it}Dit​ equals one when unit iii is treated in period ttt, that is Dit=1{t≥ti}D_{it}=\mathbf{1}\{t\geq t_i\}Dit​=1{t≥ti​} because treatment is absorbing. It generalizes equation (1): the unit dummies replace TREATiTREAT_iTREATi​ and the period dummies replace POSTtPOST_tPOSTt​, which cannot be defined for control units when there is no single treatment date. With two groups and two periods the two regressions give the same coefficient.

Dit=TREATi×POSTt⟹β^DD=β^2x2.D_{it}=TREAT_i\times POST_t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\hat{\beta}^{2x2}.Dit​=TREATi​×POSTt​⟹β^​DD=β^​2x2.

The single coefficient βDD\beta^{DD}βDD imposes that the effect of treatment is one number: the same for every unit and for every length of exposure. The identifying variation is what is left in DitD_{it}Dit​ after removing unit and period means, which is made explicit in equation (4). Nothing in the regression says which units serve as controls for which. The note answers this question: equation (9) shows that the estimate is a weighted average of all 2x2 comparisons, including comparisons in which already-treated units are the controls, and equation (15) shows that the probability limit is VWATT+VWCT−ΔATT\text{VWATT}+\text{VWCT}-\Delta\text{ATT}VWATT+VWCT−ΔATT, so the homogeneity built into the specification matters for the interpretation.

This defines the building block of every 2x2 comparison: a mean outcome of one timing group over one window of time. The term in square brackets is the cross-sectional mean in period ttt of the units whose treatment date is bbb. The outer sum averages these period means over the periods t=a,…,Tt=a,\ldots,Tt=a,…,T, which are the post-period of a treatment date aaa. There are T−(a−1)T-(a-1)T−(a−1) such periods, which explains the divisor. The two indices play different roles: the subscript bbb says whose outcomes are averaged and the superscript window says when. They coincide when a group is evaluated over its own post-period and differ when a group serves as a control over the window of another group.

The window lengths are linked to the shares of time treated, since Dˉa=(T−(a−1))/T\bar{D}_a=(T-(a-1))/TDˉa​=(T−(a−1))/T. The other two means used in the note are defined in the same way:

yˉbPRE(a)≡1a−1∑t=1a−1[∑iyit1{ti=b}∑i1{ti=b}],yˉbMID(k,ℓ)≡1ℓ−k∑t=kℓ−1[∑iyit1{ti=b}∑i1{ti=b}].\bar{y}^{\text{PRE}(a)}_b\equiv\frac{1}{a-1}\sum_{t=1}^{a-1}\left[\frac{\sum_iy_{it}\mathbf{1}\{t_i=b\}}{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{t_i=b\}}\right],\qquad\bar{y}^{\text{MID}(k,\ell)}_b\equiv\frac{1}{\ell-k}\sum_{t=k}^{\ell-1}\left[\frac{\sum_iy_{it}\mathbf{1}\{t_i=b\}}{\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{t_i=b\}}\right].yˉ​bPRE(a)​≡a−11​t=1∑a−1​[∑i​1{ti​=b}∑i​yit​1{ti​=b}​],yˉ​bMID(k,ℓ)​≡ℓ−k1​t=k∑ℓ−1​[∑i​1{ti​=b}∑i​yit​1{ti​=b}​].

As shares of the panel, PRE(k)\text{PRE}(k)PRE(k) has length 1−Dˉk1-\bar{D}_k1−Dˉk​, MID(k,ℓ)\text{MID}(k,\ell)MID(k,ℓ) has length Dˉk−Dˉℓ\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ellDˉk​−Dˉℓ​ and POST(ℓ)\text{POST}(\ell)POST(ℓ) has length Dˉℓ\bar{D}_\ellDˉℓ​. Because the regression averages over windows and not over single periods, the treatment effect parameter in equation (12) is also a window average. The window means enter equations (5), (6) and (7).

Start from equation (2) and apply the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem: the coefficient on DitD_{it}Dit​ equals the coefficient from regressing yity_{it}yit​ on the residual of DitD_{it}Dit​ after projecting it on the unit and period dummies. In a balanced panel the fitted value of that projection is the unit mean plus the period mean minus the grand mean, so the residual is

D~it=Dit−(Dˉi+Dˉt−Dˉˉ)=(Dit−Dˉi)−(Dˉt−Dˉˉ).\tilde{D}_{it}=D_{it}-\left(\bar{D}_i+\bar{D}_t-\bar{\bar{D}}\right)=\left(D_{it}-\bar{D}_i\right)-\left(\bar{D}_t-\bar{\bar{D}}\right).D~it​=Dit​−(Dˉi​+Dˉt​−Dˉˉ)=(Dit​−Dˉi​)−(Dˉt​−Dˉˉ).

To confirm that this is the residual, check that it is orthogonal to every dummy. Summing over periods for a given unit and over units for a given period gives

∑tD~it=TDˉi−TDˉi−TDˉˉ+TDˉˉ=0,∑iD~it=NDˉt−NDˉˉ−NDˉt+NDˉˉ=0.\sum_t\tilde{D}_{it}=T\bar{D}_i-T\bar{D}_i-T\bar{\bar{D}}+T\bar{\bar{D}}=0,\qquad\sum_i\tilde{D}_{it}=N\bar{D}_t-N\bar{\bar{D}}-N\bar{D}_t+N\bar{\bar{D}}=0.t∑​D~it​=TDˉi​−TDˉi​−TDˉˉ+TDˉˉ=0,i∑​D~it​=NDˉt​−NDˉˉ−NDˉt​+NDˉˉ=0.

The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell coefficient is the ratio of the sum of cross products to the sum of squares of the residual:

β^DD=∑i∑tyitD~it∑i∑tD~it2.\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\frac{\sum_i\sum_ty_{it}\tilde{D}_{it}}{\sum_i\sum_t\tilde{D}^2_{it}}.β^​DD=∑i​∑t​D~it2​∑i​∑t​yit​D~it​​.

The outcome does not need to be demeaned, because the two orthogonality conditions imply that any unit-specific or period-specific component of yity_{it}yit​ has zero cross product with D~it\tilde{D}_{it}D~it​:

∑i∑t(yˉi+yˉt−yˉˉ)D~it=0⟹∑i∑tyitD~it=∑i∑ty~itD~it.\sum_i\sum_t\left(\bar{y}_i+\bar{y}_t-\bar{\bar{y}}\right)\tilde{D}_{it}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_i\sum_ty_{it}\tilde{D}_{it}=\sum_i\sum_t\tilde{y}_{it}\tilde{D}_{it}.i∑​t∑​(yˉ​i​+yˉ​t​−yˉ​ˉ​)D~it​=0⟹i∑​t∑​yit​D~it​=i∑​t∑​y~​it​D~it​.

Dividing numerator and denominator by NTNTNT gives the equation. Since D~it\tilde{D}_{it}D~it​ has mean zero, the numerator is the sample covariance C^(yit,D~it)\hat{C}(y_{it},\tilde{D}_{it})C^(yit​,D~it​) and the denominator is the variance V^D\hat{V}^DV^D. All later results come from rewriting this numerator.

This is the treated versus untreated 2x2 DD: the estimate one would obtain by keeping only timing group jjj and the untreated group UUU and running the regression of equation (2), which in that subsample coincides with equation (1). The first parenthesis is the change in the mean outcome of group jjj from the periods before its treatment date to the periods from that date onward. The second parenthesis is the change in the mean outcome of the untreated group between the same two windows, which estimates what would have happened to group jjj without treatment. The windows are defined by the treatment date of the treated group, so the comparison with group kkk uses a different split of the panel than the comparison with group ℓ\ellℓ.

It uses all TTT periods and the share nj+nUn_j+n_Unj​+nU​ of the units. Equation (14) shows that its probability limit is ATTj(POST(j))\text{ATT}_j(\text{POST}(j))ATTj​(POST(j)) plus the difference in untreated trends between group jjj and group UUU, so it is a clean comparison under common trends even when treatment effects change over time. In the three-group numerical example, where effects are constant, these terms equal 10 for group kkk and 15 for group ℓ\ellℓ. They enter the decomposition in equation (9) with the weights skUs_{kU}skU​ of equation (10). Units that are treated in every period of the panel enter in the same way as untreated units, because their treatment status never changes.

This is the earlier versus later 2x2 DD. It uses only the periods before ℓ\ellℓ, in which the late group is not yet treated and is a valid untreated control. Within that window the early group switches from untreated in PRE(k)\text{PRE}(k)PRE(k) to treated in MID(k,ℓ)\text{MID}(k,\ell)MID(k,ℓ). The first parenthesis is the change in the mean outcome of the early group between these two windows, and the second is the change for the late group over the same windows.

The subsample contains the share nk+nℓn_k+n_\ellnk​+nℓ​ of the units and the share 1−Dˉℓ1-\bar{D}_\ell1−Dˉℓ​ of the periods. Within it, group kkk is treated for the fraction

Dˉk−Dˉℓ1−Dˉℓ\frac{\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell}{1-\bar{D}_\ell}1−Dˉℓ​Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​​

of the periods, which is why this ratio appears in the variance in equation (8). Both groups are untreated in the pre-window and only the treatment group is treated in the post-window, so the comparison has the structure of equation (5). Equation (14) shows that it identifies ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))\text{ATT}_k(\text{MID}(k,\ell))ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ)) under common trends in untreated outcomes between the two groups. The effect is averaged over the first ℓ−k\ell-kℓ−k periods of exposure only, so when effects grow with exposure this term picks up short-run effects. In the trend-break example of equation (20) it equals ϕ(ℓ−k+1)/2\phi(\ell-k+1)/2ϕ(ℓ−k+1)/2. Its weight in the decomposition is skℓks^k_{k\ell}skℓk​ in equation (10).

This is the later versus earlier 2x2 DD. It uses only the periods from kkk onward. Within that window the late group switches from untreated in MID(k,ℓ)\text{MID}(k,\ell)MID(k,ℓ) to treated in POST(ℓ)\text{POST}(\ell)POST(ℓ), while the early group is treated throughout. The first parenthesis is the change in the mean outcome of the late group, and the second is the change in the mean outcome of the early group, which acts as the control because its treatment status does not change.

The subsample contains the share nk+nℓn_k+n_\ellnk​+nℓ​ of the units and the share Dˉk\bar{D}_kDˉk​ of the periods, and within it the late group is treated for the fraction Dˉℓ/Dˉk\bar{D}_\ell/\bar{D}_kDˉℓ​/Dˉk​ of the periods. This term is the source of the main problem studied in the paper. The change in the outcome of the control group contains the change in its own treatment effect between the two windows, so by equation (14)

βkℓ2x2,ℓ=ATTℓ(POST(ℓ))−[ATTk(POST(ℓ))−ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))]\beta^{2x2,\ell}_{k\ell}=\text{ATT}_\ell\left(\text{POST}(\ell)\right)-\left[\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{POST}(\ell)\right)-\text{ATT}_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)\right]βkℓ2x2,ℓ​=ATTℓ​(POST(ℓ))−[ATTk​(POST(ℓ))−ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ))]

when untreated trends are common. If the effect in group kkk is constant over time the bracket is zero and the comparison is valid. If the effect grows, the bracket is positive and the term is biased downward, and it can be negative when every effect is positive, as in equation (20). The term enters equation (9) with weight skℓℓs^\ell_{k\ell}skℓℓ​, and the brackets of all such terms add up to ΔATT\Delta\text{ATT}ΔATT in equation (18). In the application these terms have a total weight of 0.26 and average 3.51 while all the other types are negative.

Each line is the variance of the two-way demeaned treatment dummy computed inside a 2x2 subsample. Consider a generic subsample with two groups: group aaa with relative size nabn_{ab}nab​, treated in a fraction ddd of the subsample periods, and group bbb whose treatment status is a constant ccc (zero if not yet treated or untreated, one if already treated). d=Dˉk−Dˉℓ1−Dˉℓ,1−d=1−Dˉk1−Dˉℓ.d=\frac{\bar{D}_k-\bar{D}_\ell}{1-\bar{D}_\ell},\qquad1-d=\frac{1-\bar{D}_k}{1-\bar{D}_\ell}.d=1−Dˉℓ​Dˉk​−Dˉℓ​​,1−d=1−Dˉℓ​1−Dˉk​​.

Start from the numerator of equation (4). This is the treatment effect parameter that a 2x2 DD can identify. The expectation is the average effect in period ttt of being treated at date kkk, compared with not being treated, for the units actually treated at date kkk. The effect may depend on the group kkk, on calendar time ttt and on the time since treatment t−kt-kt−k. The parameter averages these period-specific effects with equal weights over the TWT_WTW​ periods of a window WWW. It is a window average because the estimators in equations (5), (6) and (7) are differences of window means.

Three versions appear in equation (14): ATTk(POST(k))\text{ATT}_k(\text{POST}(k))ATTk​(POST(k)), the effect of group kkk over its whole post-period; ATTk(MID(k,ℓ))\text{ATT}_k(\text{MID}(k,\ell))ATTk​(MID(k,ℓ)), its effect over the first ℓ−k\ell-kℓ−k periods of exposure; and ATTk(POST(ℓ))\text{ATT}_k(\text{POST}(\ell))ATTk​(POST(ℓ)), its effect in later periods, which matters when group kkk is a control. The first is a weighted average of the other two:

If effects do not change over time all three coincide, which is the case of equation (19). If effects grow with exposure, the middle-window parameter is smaller than the post-window parameter, so different 2x2 DDs estimate different numbers, and the difference between the last two is the bias term in equation (18). With a linear trend-break of slope ϕ\phiϕ the effect after eee periods of exposure is ϕe\phi eϕe and the window parameter is ϕ\phiϕ times the average exposure in the window, as used in equation (20).

This is the change in the average untreated potential outcome of timing group kkk between an earlier window W0W_0W0​ and a later window W1W_1W1​. It describes what would have happened to the group without treatment. For the periods in which the group is treated it is a counterfactual quantity and cannot be observed, so statements about it are assumptions.

Its role is to state common trends precisely. In equation (14) each 2x2 DD equals a treatment effect plus the difference of this quantity between the treatment group and the control group over the two windows of the comparison. A 2x2 DD is unbiased by trends when the two groups have the same change, whatever its size, for example

ΔYk0(POST(k),PRE(k))=ΔYU0(POST(k),PRE(k)).\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{POST}(k),\text{PRE}(k)\right)=\Delta Y^0_U\left(\text{POST}(k),\text{PRE}(k)\right).ΔYk0​(POST(k),PRE(k))=ΔYU0​(POST(k),PRE(k)).

The windows matter: the same pair of groups can have equal changes between one pair of windows and unequal changes between another. If the average untreated outcome of group kkk follows a linear trend, the mean over a window of consecutive periods equals the value at the midpoint of the window, so the change is the slope times the distance between the midpoints of W1W_1W1​ and W0W_0W0​. That distance is T/2T/2T/2 for POST(k)\text{POST}(k)POST(k) against PRE(k)\text{PRE}(k)PRE(k), (ℓ−1)/2(\ell-1)/2(ℓ−1)/2 for MID(k,ℓ)\text{MID}(k,\ell)MID(k,ℓ) against PRE(k)\text{PRE}(k)PRE(k) and (T−k+1)/2(T-k+1)/2(T−k+1)/2 for POST(ℓ)\text{POST}(\ell)POST(ℓ) against MID(k,ℓ)\text{MID}(k,\ell)MID(k,ℓ). These distances are used in the derivation of equation (22). The weighted sum of all such differences is VWCT in equation (17).

These are the three terms defined in equations (16), (17) and (18). The weights sum to one, so VWATT is a proper weighted average of treatment effects. The estimate has a causal interpretation as VWATT only if the other two terms vanish: VWCT=0\text{VWCT}=0VWCT=0 is a restriction on untreated trends, while ΔATT=0\Delta\text{ATT}=0ΔATT=0 is a restriction on treatment effects themselves, namely that they do not change over time in groups that serve as already-treated controls.

VWATT collects the treatment effect part of every 2x2 DD in equation (14), weighted by the limit weights of equation (10). There is one average effect per 2x2 comparison, and it belongs to the treatment group of that comparison over the post-window of that comparison: the whole post-period for comparisons with untreated units, the middle window for earlier versus later comparisons and the window after ℓ\ellℓ for later versus earlier comparisons. All weights are positive and they sum to one, so VWATT lies between the smallest and the largest of these window effects. It is the part of the estimand in equation (15) that one would like to recover.

Two features distinguish it from a sample average effect on the treated. First, the weights reflect the variance of treatment and not only group size: groups treated near the middle of the panel count more, by equation (10). Second, the same group appears several times with different windows, so short-run effects from the middle windows are up-weighted when effects change with exposure. With constant effects by group, equation (19) gives the weight of each group. The three-group example illustrates the first feature: the effects are 10 and 15, the groups are equally large, and

VWATT=(0.37+0.28)×10+(0.22+0.13)×15≈11.75<12.5.\text{VWATT}=\left(0.37+0.28\right)\times10+\left(0.22+0.13\right)\times15\approx11.75<12.5.VWATT=(0.37+0.28)×10+(0.22+0.13)×15≈11.75<12.5.

The value differs from the equally weighted average because the early group is treated closer to the middle of the panel. Lengthening the panel changes the weights and moves the value to about 13.4 although no effect has changed.

VWCT collects the trend part of every 2x2 DD in equation (14) with the same weights as VWATT. Each term is a difference between the treatment group and the control group of one comparison in the change of average untreated potential outcomes, as defined in equation (13), over the two windows of that comparison. In the first line the control is the untreated group, in the second the later group before its treatment, and in the third the earlier group, whose untreated trend still matters although it is already treated.

The identifying assumption of the regression is VWCT=0\text{VWCT}=0VWCT=0. This is weaker than common trends in every pair, because differential trends of opposite sign can cancel in the weighted sum, but the usual argument for the assumption is pairwise common trends, which makes every term zero. The expression also shows that the untreated trend of one timing group enters many terms: with a positive sign where the group is the treatment group and a negative sign where it is the control. Under linear trends these contributions can be netted out, which gives equation (22): the bias caused by the trend of group kkk is proportional to wkT−wkCw^T_k-w^C_kwkT​−wkC​. A two-group case shows the offsetting signs:

VWCT=σkℓk[ΔYk0(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))−ΔYℓ0(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))]−σkℓℓ[ΔYk0(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))−ΔYℓ0(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))].\text{VWCT}=\sigma^k_{k\ell}\left[\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell),\text{PRE}(k)\right)-\Delta Y^0_\ell\left(\text{MID}(k,\ell),\text{PRE}(k)\right)\right]-\sigma^\ell_{k\ell}\left[\Delta Y^0_k\left(\text{POST}(\ell),\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)-\Delta Y^0_\ell\left(\text{POST}(\ell),\text{MID}(k,\ell)\right)\right].VWCT=σkℓk​[ΔYk0​(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))−ΔYℓ0​(MID(k,ℓ),PRE(k))]−σkℓℓ​[ΔYk0​(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))−ΔYℓ0​(POST(ℓ),MID(k,ℓ))].

A faster trend in group kkk biases the first comparison upward and the second downward.

This term collects the extra bracket of the third line of equation (14). It exists only for later versus earlier comparisons, where the already-treated group kkk is the control for group ℓ\ellℓ. The bracket is the change in the average treatment effect of group kkk between the window before ℓ\ellℓ and the window after ℓ\ellℓ, in the sense of equation (12), and its weight is the limit weight of that comparison from equation (10). It enters equation (15) with a negative sign, because the change in the outcome of a control group is subtracted in a DD.

The term is zero when the effects of every group are constant over time, whatever the heterogeneity across groups. When effects grow with exposure each bracket is positive and the estimate is pulled below VWATT; when effects fade the estimate is pulled above it. It is not a failure of common trends, since it involves treatment effects and not untreated outcomes, and it cannot be removed by adding controls for trends. The single-coefficient regression implicitly gives these effect changes a negative weight, which is the origin of the negative weights discussed in the related literature. For the linear trend-break effect of equation (20) each bracket is

which grows with the length of the post-period of the control group. In the application the later versus earlier terms have total weight 0.26 and average 3.51, and removing them moves the estimate from −3.08-3.08−3.08 to −5.44-5.44−5.44. Always-treated units used as controls generate the same kind of term with large weights.

The first term is β^DD\hat{\beta}^{DD}β^​DD; subtracting it gives the equation. It is an exact identity that requires only that both estimators are written over the same list of 2x2 comparisons, with a weight of zero for comparisons that an estimator does not use. The first term holds the baseline weights fixed and changes the 2x2 DDs, the second holds the 2x2 DDs fixed and changes the weights, and the third is the interaction. As in any decomposition of this kind the split depends on the reference point: evaluating the change in the 2x2 DDs at the alternative weights would absorb the interaction into the first term. In the application, population weighting moves the estimate by 2.73, of which 52 percent is due to the 2x2 DDs, 39 percent to the weights and 9 percent to the interaction.

This adds a vector of time-varying controls Xit\mathbf{X}_{it}Xit​ with coefficients Φ\PhiΦ to the regression of equation (2). The coefficient of interest is now βDD∣X\beta^{DD|X}βDD∣X, the coefficient on the treatment dummy conditional on the controls. Time-invariant controls would be absorbed by the unit fixed effects and controls common to all units by the period fixed effects, so only variation in the controls within units over time, relative to other units, matters.

The usual motivation is that the controls capture differential trends, so that common trends is more plausible conditional on them. The note shows that their effect is more complicated. By equations (25) and (26) the controls change the treatment variable itself: the regression uses treatment net of its linear prediction from the controls. That adjusted variable varies across units inside a timing group and period, which the treatment dummy does not, so a new source of identifying variation appears, as in equations (27) and (28). The between-group part keeps a 2x2 structure, in equation (29), but with different weights and with an adjustment based on a prediction estimated in the full sample. The final decomposition is equation (30). The specification also assumes that the controls are not themselves affected by treatment; otherwise part of the effect is netted out. In the application three controls move the estimate from −3.08-3.08−3.08 to −2.52-2.52−2.52, and most of the change comes from the within term.

This is the auxiliary regression of the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem for the controlled specification in equation (24). The dependent variable is the treatment dummy with unit and period means removed, as in equation (4), and the regressors are the controls demeaned in the same way. Γ\GammaΓ is the vector of coefficients and d~it\tilde{d}_{it}d~it​ is the residual: the part of the variation in treatment that the controls do not predict linearly. The estimated coefficient vector and the fitted value are

Γ^′=(∑i∑tX~itX~it′)−1∑i∑tX~itD~it,p~it≡Γ^X~it.\hat{\Gamma}'=\left(\sum_i\sum_t\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{it}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}'_{it}\right)^{-1}\sum_i\sum_t\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{it}\tilde{D}_{it},\qquad\tilde{p}_{it}\equiv\hat{\Gamma}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{it}.Γ^′=(i∑​t∑​X~it​X~it′​)−1i∑​t∑​X~it​D~it​,p~​it​≡Γ^X~it​.

The fitted value is a linear prediction of treatment status. It is estimated once from the whole sample, and it is not a propensity score in the usual sense, since it is linear and can lie outside the unit interval. The residual d~it=D~it−p~it\tilde{d}_{it}=\tilde{D}_{it}-\tilde{p}_{it}d~it​=D~it​−p~​it​ is the variation that identifies the controlled coefficient in equation (26). Two properties matter later. The residual is orthogonal to the fitted value by construction, so its variance is smaller than that of the adjusted dummy. And while the adjusted dummy is the same for all units of a timing group in a period, the prediction differs across those units whenever their covariate paths differ, which is the reason for the split in equation (27). In the application the R-squared of this regression is 0.0067, so the controls barely change the treatment variable.

Start from equation (24). By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem the coefficient on DitD_{it}Dit​ is obtained by regressing yity_{it}yit​ on the residual from a regression of DitD_{it}Dit​ on all other regressors: the unit dummies, the period dummies and Xit\mathbf{X}_{it}Xit​. This projection can be done in two steps. First remove unit and period means from all variables, as in equation (4); then regress the demeaned treatment on the demeaned controls, which is equation (25). The residual of the second step is

d~it=D~it−Γ^X~it=D~it−p~it.\tilde{d}_{it}=\tilde{D}_{it}-\hat{\Gamma}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}_{it}=\tilde{D}_{it}-\tilde{p}_{it}.d~it​=D~it​−Γ^X~it​=D~it​−p~​it​.

It is orthogonal to the unit dummies and the period dummies, because both of its parts are two-way demeaned, and to the demeaned controls by the normal equations of the second step. The coefficient is therefore the ratio of the cross product with the outcome to the sum of squares:

Between term. By the derivation of equation (27) the between component is the adjusted dummy minus the between component of predicted treatment, and the adjusted dummy has no within component. Therefore

C^(yit,d~kt)=C^(yit,D~it)−C^(yit,p~kt)=β^DDV^D−β^bpV^bp,\begin{aligned} \hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt}\right)&=\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{D}_{it}\right)-\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{p}_{kt}\right)\\ &=\hat{\beta}^{DD}\hat{V}^D-\hat{\beta}^p_b\hat{V}^p_b, \end{aligned}C^(yit​,d~kt​)​=C^(yit​,D~it​)−C^(yit​,p~​kt​)=β^​DDV^D−β^​bp​V^bp​,​

where the first product uses equation (4) and the second defines β^bp≡C^(yit,p~kt)/V^bp\hat{\beta}^p_b\equiv\hat{C}(y_{it},\tilde{p}_{kt})/\hat{V}^p_bβ^​bp​≡C^(yit​,p~​kt​)/V^bp​, the coefficient of a regression of the outcome on the between component of predicted treatment, which is already two-way demeaned. Multiplying and dividing each covariance by the variance of its component,

β^DD∣X=V^wdV^dβ^wp+V^bdV^d[β^DDV^D−β^bpV^bpV^bd].\hat{\beta}^{DD|X}=\frac{\hat{V}^d_w}{\hat{V}^d}\hat{\beta}^p_w+\frac{\hat{V}^d_b}{\hat{V}^d}\left[\frac{\hat{\beta}^{DD}\hat{V}^D-\hat{\beta}^p_b\hat{V}^p_b}{\hat{V}^d_b}\right].β^​DD∣X=V^dV^wd​​β^​wp​+V^dV^bd​​[V^bd​β^​DDV^D−β^​bp​V^bp​​].

The term in square brackets is the between coefficient β^bd=C^(yit,d~kt)/V^bd\hat{\beta}^d_b=\hat{C}(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt})/\hat{V}^d_bβ^​bd​=C^(yit​,d~kt​)/V^bd​. Since V^d=V^wd+V^bd\hat{V}^d=\hat{V}^d_w+\hat{V}^d_bV^d=V^wd​+V^bd​ by the orthogonality shown for equation (27), the two factors are Ω\OmegaΩ and 1−Ω1-\Omega1−Ω and the controlled coefficient is a variance-weighted average of a within and a between coefficient. The uncontrolled estimate appears inside the between coefficient, but it is rescaled by V^D/V^bd\hat{V}^D/\hat{V}^d_bV^D/V^bd​ and corrected by the relationship between the outcome and predicted treatment. In the application the within share is small but the within coefficient is 80.01, and their product, about 0.40, accounts for most of the change caused by the controls.

Start from the numerator of the between coefficient, C^(yit,d~kt)\hat{C}(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt})C^(yit​,d~kt​). The between component varies only by timing group and period and averages to zero across groups in each period, which are the two properties used in the derivation of equation (9). The same collapse to group means and the same lemma therefore give a sum over all pairs of groups, including pairs with the untreated group:

C^(yit,d~kt)=∑k∑ℓ>knknℓ{1T∑t(yˉkt−yˉℓt)[(dˉkt−dˉk)−(dˉℓt−dˉℓ)]}.\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt}\right)=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}n_kn_\ell\left\{\frac{1}{T}\sum_t\left(\bar{y}_{kt}-\bar{y}_{\ell t}\right)\left[\left(\bar{d}_{kt}-\bar{d}_k\right)-\left(\bar{d}_{\ell t}-\bar{d}_\ell\right)\right]\right\}.C^(yit​,d~kt​)=k∑​ℓ>k∑​nk​nℓ​{T1​t∑​(yˉ​kt​−yˉ​ℓt​)[(dˉkt​−dˉk​)−(dˉℓt​−dˉℓ​)]}.

In the subsample that contains only groups kkk and ℓ\ellℓ, two-way demeaning of the group-by-period mean gives (1−nkℓ)(1-n_{k\ell})(1−nkℓ​) times the bracket for group kkk and −nkℓ-n_{k\ell}−nkℓ​ times the bracket for group ℓ\ellℓ, by the argument used for equation (8). The covariance of the outcome with the between component in that subsample, denoted C^kℓ\hat{C}_{k\ell}C^kℓ​, is therefore nkℓ(1−nkℓ)n_{k\ell}(1-n_{k\ell})nkℓ​(1−nkℓ​) times the term in braces. Since nknℓ=(nk+nℓ)2nkℓ(1−nkℓ)n_kn_\ell=(n_k+n_\ell)^2n_{k\ell}(1-n_{k\ell})nk​nℓ​=(nk​+nℓ​)2nkℓ​(1−nkℓ​),

C^(yit,d~kt)=∑k∑ℓ>k(nk+nℓ)2C^kℓ(yit,d~kt).\hat{C}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt}\right)=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)^2\hat{C}_{k\ell}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt}\right).C^(yit​,d~kt​)=k∑​ℓ>k∑​(nk​+nℓ​)2C^kℓ​(yit​,d~kt​).

Inside the subsample split the between component as in the derivation of equation (28), into the adjusted dummy minus predicted treatment, and write each covariance as a variance times a coefficient:

C^kℓ(yit,d~kt)=C^kℓ(yit,D~kt)−C^kℓ(yit,p~kt)=V^kℓDβ^kℓ2x2−V^b,kℓpβ^b,kℓp.\hat{C}_{k\ell}\left(y_{it},\tilde{d}_{kt}\right)=\hat{C}_{k\ell}\left(y_{it},\tilde{D}_{kt}\right)-\hat{C}_{k\ell}\left(y_{it},\tilde{p}_{kt}\right)=\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}-\hat{V}^p_{b,k\ell}\hat{\beta}^p_{b,k\ell}.C^kℓ​(yit​,d~kt​)=C^kℓ​(yit​,D~kt​)−C^kℓ​(yit​,p~​kt​)=V^kℓD​β^​kℓ2x2​−V^b,kℓp​β^​b,kℓp​.

Here V^kℓDβ^kℓ2x2\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}V^kℓD​β^​kℓ2x2​ is the numerator of the uncontrolled two-group estimator of equation (11), or of equation (5) when one group is untreated. Dividing by V^bd\hat{V}^d_bV^bd​ and multiplying and dividing each pair by V^b,kℓd\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}V^b,kℓd​ gives the equation:

β^bd=∑k∑ℓ>k(nk+nℓ)2V^b,kℓdV^bd⏟skℓb∣X[V^kℓDβ^kℓ2x2−V^b,kℓpβ^b,kℓpV^b,kℓd]⏟β^b,kℓd.\hat{\beta}^d_b=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}\underbrace{\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)^2\frac{\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}}{\hat{V}^d_b}}_{s^{b|X}_{k\ell}}\underbrace{\left[\frac{\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}-\hat{V}^p_{b,k\ell}\hat{\beta}^p_{b,k\ell}}{\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}}\right]}_{\hat{\beta}^d_{b,k\ell}}.β^​bd​=k∑​ℓ>k∑​skℓb∣X​(nk​+nℓ​)2V^bd​V^b,kℓd​​​​β^​b,kℓd​[V^b,kℓd​V^kℓD​β^​kℓ2x2​−V^b,kℓp​β^​b,kℓp​​]​​.

Applying the first display with the between component in place of the outcome shows that V^bd=∑k∑ℓ>k(nk+nℓ)2V^b,kℓd\hat{V}^d_b=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}(n_k+n_\ell)^2\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}V^bd​=∑k​∑ℓ>k​(nk​+nℓ​)2V^b,kℓd​, so the weights sum to one. The pairwise terms cannot be split further into earlier versus later and later versus earlier parts, because the difference between two groups in the between component is no longer constant within the three windows.

Combine the last two results. Equation (28) writes the controlled coefficient as a weighted average of the within coefficient and the between coefficient, with Ω≡V^wd/V^d\Omega\equiv\hat{V}^d_w/\hat{V}^dΩ≡V^wd​/V^d and 1−Ω=V^bd/V^d1-\Omega=\hat{V}^d_b/\hat{V}^d1−Ω=V^bd​/V^d, which sum to one because the within and between components are orthogonal:

β^DD∣X=Ωβ^wp+(1−Ω)β^bd.\hat{\beta}^{DD|X}=\Omega\hat{\beta}^p_w+\left(1-\Omega\right)\hat{\beta}^d_b.β^​DD∣X=Ωβ^​wp​+(1−Ω)β^​bd​.

Equation (29) writes the between coefficient as a weighted average over pairs of groups of adjusted 2x2 terms:

β^bd=∑k∑ℓ>kskℓb∣Xβ^b,kℓd,skℓb∣X=(nk+nℓ)2V^b,kℓdV^bd,β^b,kℓd=V^kℓDβ^kℓ2x2−V^b,kℓpβ^b,kℓpV^b,kℓd.\hat{\beta}^d_b=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}s^{b|X}_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^d_{b,k\ell},\qquad s^{b|X}_{k\ell}=\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)^2\frac{\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}}{\hat{V}^d_b},\qquad\hat{\beta}^d_{b,k\ell}=\frac{\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}-\hat{V}^p_{b,k\ell}\hat{\beta}^p_{b,k\ell}}{\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}}.β^​bd​=k∑​ℓ>k∑​skℓb∣X​β^​b,kℓd​,skℓb∣X​=(nk​+nℓ​)2V^bd​V^b,kℓd​​,β^​b,kℓd​=V^b,kℓd​V^kℓD​β^​kℓ2x2​−V^b,kℓp​β^​b,kℓp​​.

Substituting the second into the first and writing β^kℓ2x2∣d\hat{\beta}^{2x2|d}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2∣d​ for β^b,kℓd\hat{\beta}^d_{b,k\ell}β^​b,kℓd​ gives the equation. It is the counterpart with controls of equation (9). Setting the controls aside makes predicted treatment zero, so Ω=0\Omega=0Ω=0, the adjusted variances equal V^kℓD\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}V^kℓD​ and the adjusted terms equal β^kℓ2x2\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell}β^​kℓ2x2​:

β^DD=∑k∑ℓ>k(nk+nℓ)2V^kℓDV^Dβ^kℓ2x2,\hat{\beta}^{DD}=\sum_k\sum_{\ell>k}\left(n_k+n_\ell\right)^2\frac{\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}}{\hat{V}^D}\hat{\beta}^{2x2}_{k\ell},β^​DD=k∑​ℓ>k∑​(nk​+nℓ​)2V^DV^kℓD​​β^​kℓ2x2​,

which is equation (9) with each timing pair combined by the weight μkℓ\mu_{k\ell}μkℓ​ of equation (11). Comparing the two shows the three channels through which controls change the estimate: a within term with weight Ω\OmegaΩ that has no counterpart without controls, weights based on V^b,kℓd\hat{V}^d_{b,k\ell}V^b,kℓd​ instead of V^kℓD\hat{V}^D_{k\ell}V^kℓD​, and 2x2 terms that subtract the pairwise relationship between the outcome and predicted treatment. In the application these account for 73, 5 and 22 percent of the change of 0.56 in the estimate.
